prompt.en: Two stations confirm a contact near midnight, one in Atlantic Canada and one in British Columbia. Which log habit best prevents later date confusion?

text.en: Record the UTC date as well as the UTC time for the contact.
Use only the local date of the operator who sent the louder signal.
Omit the date if both stations remember the band.
Let each station choose any date because confirmations do not compare dates.

explanation.en: UTC works best when the date and time travel together. Near local midnight, the same contact may fall on different local dates for different operators.

prompt.en: Which statement is NOT true about useful contact records and confirmations?

text.en: A confirmation should identify enough contact details to match both stations’ records.
Log notes can help compare a later interference complaint with your actual operating times.
Web-based systems can serve a confirmation role for many operators.
A friendly card with no contact details proves a radio contact just as well as a complete confirmation.

explanation.en: A confirmation is valuable because it ties the proof to a specific contact. Missing date, time, band, or station details makes the proof weak.

prompt.en: After trying a long-path opening, an operator writes only “beam turned around” in the log. What would improve the note?

text.en: Record the actual bearing used and mark it as the long-path trial.
Erase the short-path bearing because only the successful direction matters.
Replace the bearing with the UTC offset, because time zones define antenna direction.
Write the signal report only; antenna direction never helps future planning.

explanation.en: A useful operating note records the direction that was tested and why. That makes the log helpful when the same path or season appears again.
